title: Hemkunt Sahib
hookLine: a high Himalayan lake linked by tradition to the Tenth Guru's former life

cards: For part of every year, snow closes the path. When it opens, pilgrims climb on foot or on ponies, up a steep trail in the Himalayas, past waterfalls and wildflowers, breathing hard in the thin air.
At the top there's a lake, clear and very cold, ringed by peaks, and on its shore a gurdwara. Some pilgrims step into that icy water.
The place is called Hemkunt Sahib, and Sikh tradition ties it to a life before the Tenth Guru's life.

teach.b: First, the text. In the Bachittar Natak, a work in the Dasam Granth that Sikh tradition attributes to Guru Gobind Singh, the poet tells his own story.

In paraphrase: in an earlier life, he did deep austerity on a mountain called Hemkunt, a place of peaks, absorbed in God, until God called him to be born into the world and spread the right way of living.
He did not want to come, his mind was so joined to God's feet, but God sent him. Second, the finding. The poem names Hemkunt but gives no map.
Long after the Guru, Sikhs identified this Himalayan lake as the Hemkunt of the poem, and a gurdwara was built on its shore. Third, the honest part. Sikhs hold different views here.
Some read the passage as the Guru's literal memory of a former life; some read it as poetry about a calling. Some Sikhs also discuss which parts of the Dasam Granth are the Guru's own.
This path describes these views; it doesn't decide. Fourth, what the pilgrims do with it.
Whatever they think of the map, they climb a hard trail anyway.
At the top, the poem's picture becomes something you can stand in: a still place, high up, close to the sky, where someone, tradition says, was so happy with God that he didn't want to leave.
And left anyway, because he was sent.

how: When the snow clears, Sikh pilgrims climb the steep trail to Hemkunt Sahib, bathe in the cold lake, and join the Ardas and kirtan at the gurdwara on its shore.

practice: See the water, very still and clear, the color of the sky, with white-topped peaks all around, and let the cold, thin air slow your breath on its own. Sit at the edge with nothing to do.
Then remember the poem, someone happy in a place like this, called down into the busy world, and let your breath carry a little of the stillness down with you.
